Here’s the real formula I use inside my Microbakery Blueprint 👇
1️⃣ Add up every ingredient and packaging cost per item.
2️⃣ Multiply your total anywhere from 2.5× to 5× depending on the product.
 → Simpler items like mixes or pecans = closer to 2.5×
 → Labor-heavy goods like cookies, sourdough, or bundles = 4–5×
3️⃣ That’s your retail price - and yes, it should include your time, utilities, and profit.

Because you’re not just baking - you’re building something sustainable.

Can we stop treating a storefront like it’s the finish line for every microbakery?

Growth can look like a storefront.
But it can also look like selling out of your home kitchen, adding another pickup day, increasing your production, building wholesale accounts, launching products, teaching, hiring help - or simply creating a business that supports the life you actually want.

I’ve built Kimpton Farms from my home for more than three years, and one thing I’ve learned is that bigger isn’t automatically better.

The goal isn’t to build the bakery everyone else thinks you should have.

It’s to build a business that’s profitable, sustainable and works for your life.

A storefront is one path.
It isn’t the definition of success.

A $60 loaf of bread went viral - but the lesson for microbakers isn’t that we should all start charging $60. 🥖

It’s about understanding why people are willing to pay more for certain products - and what that can teach us about pricing our own.

Your price has to make sense for your costs, your labor, your overhead, your market and your business model.

For Kimpton Farms, I use:

Ingredients + Packaging + Labor × 2.5

That multiplier works for my business. It isn’t a universal formula every baker needs to follow.

But pricing isn’t only about plugging numbers into a calculator, either.

Customers also have to understand the value behind what they’re buying - the ingredients, fermentation, craftsmanship, experience and care that go into an artisan product.

You don’t need to be the cheapest baker in your market.

And you definitely don’t need a viral $60 loaf.

Know your costs. Understand your market. Communicate your value.

Because the goal isn’t to sell a sixty-dollar loaf of bread.

The goal is to build a bakery that’s actually profitable and sustainable for YOU. 🤎

How much should you actually pay yourself as a microbaker? And how do you figure out labor when you’re just starting out?

Let’s break it down with a real-world example.

In this video, I’m walking you through how to:

• Choose a realistic hourly labor rate based on your experience and local market
• Calculate your actual hands-on labor per loaf
• Add labor into your product cost
• Use my ingredients + packaging + labor × 2.5 pricing formula
• Sanity-check the final number against comparable products in your local market

And remember-the number a pricing formula gives you is a starting point, not an automatic selling price.

Your labor rate can change. Your efficiency will change. Your costs will change. And your pricing can change right along with your business.

The goal isn’t perfect pricing. It’s pricing that is realistic and sustainable for where your microbakery is right now.
